judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass H.B. 493, which made a person who has been finally convicted of a first- or second-degree felony ineligible to serve as a poll watcher, on top of the existing bar on a felony conviction connected to election conduct, and required the appointee's certificate of appointment to carry an affidavit that they have no such conviction. It passed the Texas House 86-52 and became law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against passing H.B. 493, which made a person who has been finally convicted of a first- or second-degree felony ineligible to serve as a poll watcher, on top of the existing bar on a felony conviction connected to election conduct, and required the appointee's certificate of appointment to carry an affidavit that they have no such conviction. It passed the Texas House 86-52 and became law.

The Texas Senate adopted the report 23-8 and the bill became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass H.B. 521, which required a curbside voter to sign a sworn statement that they cannot enter the polling place without assistance or are requesting a disability accommodation, extended curbside ballot delivery to a voter escorting such a person, required two election officers to deliver the ballot where four or more are present, barred electioneering within 20 feet of a designated curbside space, and made it a Class A misdemeanor for a person who transported seven or more curbside voters to intentionally fail to file the required form. It passed the Texas House 84-54 and became law.

It passed the Texas House 84-54 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass H.B. 5115, which raised election fraud under Section 276.013 of the Election Code from a Class A misdemeanor to a second-degree felony, to a first-degree felony when committed by an elected official, and to a third-degree felony for an attempt, and added knowingly counting votes the person knows are invalid or refusing to count votes the person knows are valid to the offense. It passed the Texas House 88-54 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 510, which let the secretary of state withhold voter-registration funding from a county voter registrar who, after written notice and a reasonable opportunity to correct, fails to timely perform an Election Code duty on approving, changing, or cancelling a registration, on scheduling or deciding a registration challenge, or on delivering a residence-confirmation notice. It passed the Texas House 109-33 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass H.B. 3053, which prohibited a municipality or county from adopting or enforcing a measure under which it organizes, sponsors, or participates in a program that buys or offers to buy firearms with the intent to remove firearms from circulation, reduce the number of firearms owned by civilians, or let people sell firearms without fear of criminal prosecution. It passed the Texas House 85-56 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 1362, which was titled the Anti-Red Flag Act and barred state and local entities from adopting or enforcing any measure relating to an extreme risk protective order unless Texas law specifically authorizes it, barred them from accepting federal grants to enforce such orders, and made serving or enforcing an extreme risk protective order not issued under Texas law a state jail felony, while leaving protective orders issued under the Family Code or the Code of Criminal Procedure untouched. It passed the Texas House 86-53 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 2284, which barred municipalities and counties from regulating archery equipment alongside firearms and air guns, made the exception that lets a municipality regulate carrying at certain public places and events inapplicable to handgun license holders, ended Type A general-law municipalities' authority to regulate firearms, and narrowed county authority to restrict bow hunting to subdivision lots smaller than seven acres rather than 10 acres or smaller. It passed the Texas House 96-43 and became law.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against passing S.B. 2284, which barred municipalities and counties from regulating archery equipment alongside firearms and air guns, made the exception that lets a municipality regulate carrying at certain public places and events inapplicable to handgun license holders, ended Type A general-law municipalities' authority to regulate firearms, and narrowed county authority to restrict bow hunting to subdivision lots smaller than seven acres rather than 10 acres or smaller. It passed the Texas House 96-43 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 11, which let a school district or open-enrollment charter school board adopt, by record vote, a policy giving students and employees a daily period for prayer and reading of the Bible or another religious text, required a signed consent form that includes an express waiver of the right to bring an Establishment Clause or related claim, barred delivery over a public address system, required the attorney general to defend an adopting district at state expense, and deleted the existing prohibition on encouraging a student to engage in or refrain from prayer. It passed the Texas House 88-48 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 965, which provided that a school district, open-enrollment charter school, or other state governmental entity may not infringe on a public school employee's right to engage in religious speech or prayer while on duty unless the infringement is necessary to further a compelling state interest and is narrowly tailored using the least restrictive means. It passed the Texas House 86-48 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 1257, which required a health benefit plan that provides or has ever provided coverage for an enrollee's gender transition procedure to also cover the adverse consequences of that procedure, annual baseline and follow-up monitoring, and any treatment needed to manage, reverse, or reconstruct from it, including for an enrollee who was not in the plan when the procedure occurred; self-funded ERISA plans are excluded. It passed the Texas House 87-58 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass H.B. 3441, which made a vaccine manufacturer liable for actual damages, court costs, and reasonable attorney's fees to a person harmed by a vaccine the manufacturer paid to advertise in Texas, with a three-year limitations period, excluding from "advertise" any discussion between a health care provider and a patient and any materials displayed in a clinical setting. It passed the Texas House 88-31 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 2337, which required a proxy advisory firm to disclose to its client, to the subject company, to the attorney general, and to the public when its voting advice is based wholly or partly on nonfinancial factors such as environmental, social, or governance goals, diversity, equity, or inclusion, or sustainability scores, or when it gives materially different advice to different clients on the same proposal, and made a violation a deceptive trade practice that an affected party may sue over. It passed the Texas House 92-50 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass S.B. 21, which created the Texas Strategic Bitcoin Reserve as a special fund outside the state treasury, managed by the comptroller, that may hold bitcoin and other cryptocurrency with an average market capitalization of at least $500 billion over the preceding 24 months, and added an advisory committee and a biennial public report. It passed the Texas House 101-42 and became law.
